task: This is a synthetic writing exercise. Using these fictional reporting notes, write a newspaper reported feature for general readers. Draw only on the supplied notes; do not invent additional reported events, scenes, or quotations. Write from this reporting snapshot as of May 19, 2025. Include a headline. Target 450 to 650 words. Follow AP style.

facts.text: DeepHeat Energy, a company founded by former oil field engineers in 2021, has drilled two enhanced geothermal test wells in the Great Basin at depths of 4.8 and 5.3 kilometers.
CEO Grace Kim said both wells reached rock temperatures above 200 degrees Celsius, sufficient for binary cycle electricity generation; neither well has yet been connected to a surface power facility.
Kim said: "We have proven the heat is there. We have proven we can reach it. The next step — creating a reservoir by fracturing the rock — is where the project either works or it doesn't."

Seismologist Dr. Marco Bianchi, who monitors induced seismicity for the project, said the fracturing phase is planned for July 2025 and will be conducted in incremental pressure stages with seismic monitoring at five surface stations and one downhole sensor.

Dr. Bianchi said: "Our protocol stops fracturing automatically if we detect anything above magnitude 2.0 on the Richter scale. Below that, we continue and review. It is a conservative protocol by industry standards."
The Great Basin site was chosen partly because of its sparse population: the nearest town has 340 residents and is 14 kilometers from the drill site.
Kim said DeepHeat's investors include three former oil company executives and a climate-focused venture fund; total investment to date is $48 million, all spent on drilling and site instrumentation.

A geothermal project in an Asian city triggered a magnitude 5.5 earthquake in 2017 and was halted after the event was linked to injection operations; Kim said DeepHeat studied that case thoroughly and identified injection rate as the key controllable variable.
Kim said: "That project injected faster than their seismic response protocol allowed them to stop. We have automated cutoffs. The human decision is whether to resume, not whether to stop."
Dr. Bianchi said the Great Basin geology is less seismically active than that affected Asian city site and that baseline seismicity monitoring over 14 months showed no events above magnitude 1.5.
DeepHeat plans to connect the first well pair to a 2-megawatt pilot turbine if fracturing creates a connected reservoir; Kim said this would be the first EGS power generation in the Great Basin.

A neighboring rancher, Tom Whitfield, 63, said he initially opposed the project but agreed to a monitoring agreement after two years of site visits and a meeting with Dr. Bianchi: "I didn't understand it. Now I understand it more. I'm not convinced it's safe. But I'm willing to watch."

Whitfield said his primary concern is water: the injection process uses water drawn from a permitted well; he wants independent verification that the project's water use does not affect his livestock well.

Dr. Bianchi said the injection well is in a different geological stratum than Whitfield's livestock well and that contamination is not physically plausible given the depth differential; he offered to provide monthly water quality testing at his own expense.

Kim said a 2-megawatt demonstration would not by itself be commercially significant: "It proves it works here. That's worth something. Commercial scale is twelve to twenty years away if we start now."
The Department of Energy funded $12 million of DeepHeat's drilling costs through the FORGE program; the remainder came from private investors.

Kim said the oil field engineers who founded DeepHeat saw geothermal as the closest application of their technical skills: "We drilled for things stored in the earth for millions of years. Heat is also stored there. The drill doesn't know the difference."

Dr. Bianchi said the fracturing result will be scientifically informative regardless of outcome: if the rock fractures as modeled, it validates EGS in this geological setting; if not, it identifies the gap.

Kim said she tells investors the most likely outcome of the July fracturing is partial success: the reservoir will exist but smaller than optimal: "Perfect first tries are for press releases. Science is iterative."
Whitfield said he plans to watch the fracturing from his truck on a ridge overlooking the site: "I've watched them drill for two years. I'm going to watch this too. Whatever happens, I was there."
